source.title: Subliminal Signals in Preference Labels
source.authors: Isotta Magistrali; Frédéric Berdoz; Sam Dauncey; Roger Wattenhofer

page_placements.theme: Selection- or judge-mediated transfer (no trait-bearing generator)

record.file_problem: None noted; the paper text appears complete.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a trait can transfer through semantically unrelated numerical data, but uses a biased judge's preference labels rather than trait-bearing teacher-generated data.
record.gate_note: The paper reports preference-transfer outcomes for numerical completions generated by a neutral student and labeled by a biased judge. Rows below record the win rates in Tables 5–7. The consistency results in Figure 2 concern evaluation of prior-work models and are not treated as this study's own intervention results. Tables 1–3 and Table 4 are left out under the row cap; details are in rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: New setting: a neutral Qwen 2.5 7B student's own number sequences are picked as preferred or dispreferred by a cat/lion/panda-biased judge, then used to train the student. The study measures whether the judge's favourite animal transfers to the student through semantically unrelated numbers. This bears on A in a variant channel (preference labels, not teacher-generated data), so T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude preference labels act as a one-bit-per-sample subliminal channel, letting a biased judge pass a trait to a neutral student via unrelated numbers. Two corrections: iterative SFT strengthened the signal while iterative DPO weakened it (Table 3). With the original model as pairwise text judge, no directional transfer appeared; only the inherently biased Cloud et al. model as judge gave some.
record.recipe_differences: The original work has a biased teacher generate trait-bearing training data for a student. This paper instead has a neutral student generate numerical completions; a biased external judge assigns preferences, and the student is aligned from those labels. Student and judge are separate instances of Qwen 2.5 7B.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with target animal, alignment procedure (SFT, DPO, iterative alignment, or SFT→DPO), and judge procedure/configuration (deep log-probability judging versus pairwise text generation; judge system prompt).

fits_no_version.finding: A biased judge's binary preference labels (one bit per pair) over a neutral student's own number sequences shift the student's favourite animal after SFT or DPO.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Judge-to-student transmission: a trait can pass through a biased judge's preference labels on semantically unrelated completions, with no trait-bearing teacher generating the data.

record.problems: The main results focus on Qwen 2.5 7B and three target animals. Cross-architecture testing is left for future work. Pairwise judging is described as preliminary and weaker or inconsistent; some panda results are weak or reversed. No harmful traits, different-base comparison, or LoRA-rank sweep is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row cap, omitted the directional preference-shift results in Appendix C, Tables 1–3, and the normal-versus-swapped win-rate results in Table 4. Table 5–7 individual normal/swapped win-rate entries were retained. The omitted tables include iterative-round preference-shift values and additional direct normal-versus-swapped comparisons.

untested.parts: The original route, a trait-bearing teacher generating the training data, is not run anew. Only released Cloud et al. students are re-evaluated (Table 5 baseline). Code and maths-reasoning data are not tested; only numbers are.
Not tested. The student and judge are both Qwen 2.5 7B. Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen 3 8B were tried for data generation but no results are reported. Cross-architecture work is left to future work.
Not tested: no mechanism analysis. The authors conjecture that the judge's prior strength matters.

Not tested. Full versus parameter-efficient fine-tuning and LoRA ranks are not reported. SFT versus DPO and iterative rounds are training-procedure variants of the channel, not the robustness axes E names.

missing.what: Re-evaluation of the released Cloud et al. teacher-data students with this study's 5-option multiple-choice evaluation. Win rates against control: cat 96%, lion 60%, panda 88%. Preference shifts: +6.52, +1.40, +4.64. Figure 2a says consistency breaks down for lion.
missing.locator: Appendix C, Table 5 and Table 1 'Baseline' rows; Figure 2a

record.verdict_notes: All rows should carry versions ["A"] only. Drop E, because SFT/DPO/iterative variants are not E's robustness axes (full fine-tuning, LoRA rank, evaluation prompt). The 50% win rate is the chance point for every win-rate row. T6/T7 rows are the pairwise-judge experiment rather than comparators. Table 5's 'SFT → DPO' cat difference is printed as 75% though 74−2=72, a typo in the source. The setup differs from A's route: the student's own outputs, filtered by a biased judge's log-probability ratio. These approximate selecting teacher-likely sequences, so the result is an analogue, not a replication.

versions.untested_parts: The original route—trait-bearing teacher-generated outputs fine-tuned by a student—is not tested; here the student's numerical outputs are labeled by a biased judge.
No different-base student–teacher/judge comparison; student and judge are separate instances of the same Qwen 2.5 7B architecture.
No misalignment or other harmful/alignment-relevant trait is tested.
The paper studies preference labels as a channel but does not test token entanglement, divergence tokens, a steering direction, or a gradient mechanism.
SFT, DPO, sequential SFT→DPO, and pairwise judging are explored. LoRA ranks are not varied, and the paper does not explicitly compare full fine-tuning against parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

relationships.condition: Deep (log-probability) judge; cat and lion under every SFT/DPO variant; panda under SFT, iterative SFT and SFT→DPO normal
relationships.reason: Normal models beat control (64–98%) while swapped models fall well below it (2–28%), showing directional transfer (T5 cat/lion rows, T5-panda-SFT-normal/-swapped, T5-panda-iterSFT-normal).
relationships.display_finding: Models trained on normal labels beat the control (64–98%), while models trained on swapped labels fell well below it (2–28%), so transfer followed the label direction.

relation.reason: The study's own results (Tables 1–7) measure whether a favourite-animal trait passes to the student through semantically unrelated numbers.

tranche.reason: This is a new setting: a biased judge selects among a neutral student's own number sequences instead of a teacher generating the data. It reports win rates for trait transfer with normal, swapped and control models. The earlier reader's T2 is also defensible, but T3 fits better because the route differs from version A's.

source_check.notes: Rows carry links to version E, but the study never varies LoRA rank, full fine-tuning or the evaluation prompt, so the E links are unsupported. Table 5's Baseline row (Cloud-style teacher-generated data) vs control reads cat 96%, lion 60%, panda 88%. Iterative alignment strengthens the signal under SFT (Table 2) but weakens it under DPO (Table 3), so the abstract's 'strengthen' holds only for SFT.

statements.correction: Table 5, deep judge. Panda SFT: normal 72%, swapped 18%. Panda iterative SFT: normal 82%, swapped 34%. So with panda's SFT variants included, swapped spans 2–34%; for cat/lion plus panda plain SFT only, it is 2–28%. Same base on both sides (Qwen 2.5 7B student and judge). The student is trained on its own judge-selected numbers, not on teacher text.
statements.problem: Normal 64–98% fits cat/lion in all five methods and panda in the SFT variants. Swapped 2–28% does not cover panda iterative SFT, whose swapped value is 34%.

statements.correction: Table 5: panda DPO normal 44%, iterative DPO normal 40%; panda swapped 56% for iterative DPO and SFT→DPO. Tables 6 and 7, original Qwen 2.5 7B judge biased by system prompt only: normal vs swapped is cat 0% and lion 12%; swapped vs control is 100% for both; normal vs control is cat 82%, lion 72%. Panda SFT→DPO normal is 74%, so DPO-based failure for panda is partial.
statements.problem: Numbers are right. 'Original neutral model' is the paper's term, but that judge carries a biased system prompt. Under it, normal models also beat control (cat 82%, lion 72%).

statements.correction: Table 5, deep judge. Cat/lion over SFT, iterative SFT, DPO, iterative DPO and SFT→DPO: normal 64–98%, swapped 2–28%. Panda: normal 40–82%, swapped 18–56% (DPO 44/28, iterative DPO 40/56, SFT→DPO 74/56, iterative SFT 82/34). Pairwise judge with DPO (Table 7): swapped vs control 36–100%.
statements.problem: The 64–98% and 2–28% ranges hold only for cat and lion (and panda plain SFT) with the deep log-probability judge. The statement gives them for SFT or DPO in general.

statements.correction: The paper says it transmits one bit per sample (Abstract, Fig. 1). The shift holds for cat and lion under SFT and DPO, and for panda under SFT. Panda under DPO and iterative DPO shows no shift (44%, 40% vs control). With a pairwise text judge (original model), normal vs swapped is 0% for cat and 12% for lion.
statements.problem: Accurate as a description, but the effect is not universal. The synthesis also files this study under version A verdicts.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Deep-judge numerical-preference setup; cat and lion, and most SFT/DPO configurations
reader_labels.reason: Normal-aligned models generally beat control while swapped-aligned models generally do not, consistent with directional trait transfer through labels (T5 rows).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Panda with DPO variants and pairwise text-generating judges
reader_labels.reason: Panda results weaken or reverse under some DPO conditions, and pairwise-judge results vary sharply by judge and animal, including high swapped-versus-control rates (T5, T6, T7 rows).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Across tested alignment methods and pairwise-judge configurations
reader_labels.reason: Transfer strength is not uniform across target animals, training methods, and judge configurations; panda and several pairwise conditions are weak or reversed (T5, T6, T7 rows).
